@@139131383 <h> The Crisis That Novelists Ca n't Handle <p> Is there any subject that fiction can not address ? From its beginnings as a form , the novel has dealt with love and hate , war and peace , courage and cowardice , boredom and catastrophe . Yet there is far more in heaven and earth than any human can convey . In the view of the writer Amitav Ghosh , one subject especially threatens to elude fiction 's comprehension . " The climate crisis , " he writes in his book-length 2016 essay , The Great Derangement , " is also a crisis of culture , and thus of the imagination . " <p> Across his many novels and nonfiction books , Ghosh has been attempting to correct this shortcoming . He has become a leading theorist of the relationship between global climate change and culture , arguing that the sparsity of the former in fiction owes to a " grid of literary forms and conventions " that coalesced just as " carbon in the atmosphere was rewriting the destiny of the earth . " Contemporary writing , he @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forces so great and impersonal that they seem to actively confound attempts at storytelling . <p> It makes sense that Ghosh would become a writer of ecological rupture , as he is , in a sense , the product of one . At some point in the mid-1850s , the river Padma suddenly carved a new path through the village of his ancestors in modern-day Bangladesh , flooding their homes and scattering them across the Indian subcontinent . As a result , Ghosh was born in Calcutta , India , in 1956 . His family 's collective memory taught him about the destructive capriciousness of the natural world , and it made him a keen observer of human migration throughout history . It also informs his skepticism of the modern realist novel . <p> In much of literary fiction , characters and settings are developed slowly , through the gradual accrual of discrete moments that rarely stray from the mundane and the reasonable . Yet this supposedly " realist " form , Ghosh argues , is in fact engaged in a " concealment of the real . " For many @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ irrevocable events . Homes flood ; tornadoes rip up crops ; fires swallow families . To be unfamiliar with these outcomes is to be the outlier , not the norm . So why , Ghosh wonders , are such rapid turnabouts so rarely present in the genre ? <p> Ghost-Eye , his 11th and latest novel , attempts to push back on this aversion to the improbable , and thus to the catastrophic -- though it fails to effectively solve the problem . In Calcutta , readers meet Varsha , a 3-year-old girl who is the youngest child of Abhay Gupta , a businessman and heir to a family that has " risen , in one generation , from modest to quite extravagant wealth . " But in September of 1969 , the toddler begins to recall another life , when she lived in an impoverished island village and ate fish . Varsha has only ever lived in a mansion and has never even visited the coast , but she insists on her recollections . This causes significant dismay among her upper-caste and strictly vegetarian Marwari Hindu family , which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the psychologist Shoma Bose . <p> Their choice is fortuitous . Though Shoma is " dogmatically materialist , " with little interest in the supernatural , she has in the past conducted research on " cases of the reincarnation type " -- young children who begin to vividly recall an existence not a bit like their own . She had embarked on this research only within the past few years , after she became the Bengali-language translator for an American researcher , Cathy Booth . Shoma initially considers it " unimaginable that reincarnation could be the subject of serious scientific research , " and her husband , Monty , calls Booth " the ghost-doctor . " But Shoma is quickly convinced of its plausibility by the subjects she meets while working with Booth . This shift sets up a narrative pattern in the novel : deep skepticism followed by immediate conversion . <p> In its opening stretch , Ghost-Eye alternates between Shoma 's 1969 consultations with the young Varsha and the experiences of Shoma 's nephew , Dinanth Datta , called Dinu by his aunt . During " the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on his childhood . He had often left the modest , overcrowded home of his family to spend time with Shoma and Monty at their large Art Deco estate , called Tavoy . His intimate , sensual memories capture the cacophony of city sounds , the tumult of left-wing agitation , and the vivid darkness of Calcutta 's periodic blackouts , " the like of which , " he notes , " I have never again experienced anywhere in the world . " These recollections are fond , but tinged with the knowledge of all that would soon change ; even the name of his city is no longer the same . <p> The novel thus proceeds in two registers , at once mysterious and elegiac . In the present , Dinu is old and lonely . He begins every day by checking the increasing concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere and a running tracker of how many species went extinct during the previous day . Shoma , even older , is bed-bound with a broken hip . Dinu 's reflections are intercut with stories from their past , memories @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ migrants and post-partition refugees who lived and worked at Tavoy . <p> Ghost-Eye is at its best when Ghosh remains in this intimate mode , following lives that persist in the face of political and ecological disruption . Yet this is the lesser part of the novelist 's plan . During the early pandemic , Dinu begins receiving FaceTime calls from Tipu , a young gay man who is working at a nonprofit in the Sundarbans , a network of coastal mangrove islands that spread across the Ganges Delta . In the nonprofit 's archives , Tipu has found a mention of a trip that Shoma made in 1969 to the islands , and he has become convinced that this visit has some cryptic connection to a project he refuses to divulge more about . <p> Ghosh has written about the Sundarbans at least twice before , in 2004 's The Hungry Tide and 2019 's Gun Island ; both Dinu and Tipu were introduced in the latter . Those novels involved investigations into history , and the past is clearly Ghosh 's comfort zone . Shoma 's investigation of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , give the first part of Ghost-Eye a satisfyingly retrospective quality . Yet Ghosh means to paint a picture not only of Dinu 's life in the 2020s , but also of the entire world , and then he aims to reach into the future . Varsha 's mysterious memories are apparently linked to a much larger set of crises , and in order to make sense of these connections , both Dinu and Ghosh will have to dispense with the material and tread into the metaphysical . <p> To say that Ghost-Eye is a novel of disaster would be underselling it . Storms smash into cities , disease shuts down whole societies , and millions of humans migrate across the globe . The scale of these events transcends the limits of any individual experience -- making it difficult for the typical realistic novel to contain them , as Ghosh has argued . <p> At the same time , natural disasters , fed and intensified by man-made climate change , are entering the realm of the familiar . In the decade since Ghosh published The Great Derangement , a few @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fiction . In Jenny Offill 's Weather , climate change intrudes on its narrator 's mundane day-to-day thoughts , a nagging anxiety that never quite boils over . Lydia Kiesling'sMobility attempts something at once more traditional and more ambitious , exploring how a young woman tries to disentangle herself from the oil industry 's poisonous tendrils . Both do a fine job of capturing how it feels to live through an age of human-engineered hazards . Yet these novels , alongside other recent works by Richard Flanagan and Alexandra Kleeman , struggle to convey what Ghosh describes in The Great Derangement as the " scalar " dimensions of the Anthropocene , an age defined by " forces of unthinkable magnitude " that both dwarf and discount any one perspective . <p> As it goes on , Ghost-Eye becomes a quest to recover ancient , repressed forces -- the supernatural powers rejected by modernity , yet still alive in the spiritualism infusing the lives of most people on the planet . In the course of her investigation , Shoma begins to suspect that Varsha is clairvoyant . The pair 's mysterious @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of parables of doubt and belief , in which a rational character is confronted by an irrational event -- and immediately convinced of its absolute truth . These conversions are not grounded in the characters that Ghosh has sketched , but rather in the plot he needs them to advance . Character gives way to contrivance , and Ghost-Eye collapses under the strain . <p> The trouble , once again , comes down to questions of scale . As Ghosh himself has noted , the " realistic " novel is loath to make space for unlikely events -- yet his solution to this problem is at odds with his own skill set . In the end , Ghosh is a very traditional novelist , adept at sketching scenes and enlivening characters with well-placed detail . But as his novel goes on , nighttime scenes and vivid memories are replaced by exchanges of purely expository dialogue , which seeks to explain to the reader , point by point , the book 's ghostly developments . This approach substitutes information for sensation , and reduces both human and supra-human experiences to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in Tipu 's video calls , where this gay Gen Zer is reduced to prompting Dinu with humiliating lines such as " Okay , Pops , since you 're trippin ' on me , I 'll spill the tea . " ) <p> Rather than creating " unbearably intimate connections , " as Ghosh has called them , between the individual and planetary scales of climate change , these tricks merely reveal the flimsiness of his narrative . The novel 's climax -- a sequence defined by reality-shattering magical spectacle -- is narrated by one character to another over FaceTime , a dreadful decision that deflates the entire story . <p> Perhaps it is n't so much the realist novel that resists catastrophe , but Ghosh 's narrow conception of the form . In The Great Derangement , he slams the avant-garde movements of the 20th century , which he believes unconsciously undermined collective narration by exalting the experience of the individual . This is a bold claim to make about modernism as a whole . Among the diverse international literatures grouped together under that heading , there are dozens @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their own . In novels such as Thousand Cranes and The Master of Go , Yasunari Kawabata wedded stream-of-consciousness to classical forms of ritual and performance , modeling rapid Japanese westernization through stories that overlay the ancient and the modern . Juan Rulfo infused his novel Pedro P ? ramo with half a century of political and economic violence , envisioning rural Mexico as a mythic space where past and present overlap . In his classic work The Obscene Bird of Night , the Chilean writer Jos ? Donoso created a literary mirror for a South America in crisis ; his mutable story 's transformations -- of subject , temporality , point of view -- replicate the developments that were roiling his home country . <p> These writers did not merely replicate modernity ; they responded to it , transforming the novel to address a world in constant and often cataclysmic flux . Artistic innovations are often driven by crises , after all , and the novel is no different . Ghosh is right to argue that naturalistic narratives are not up to the urgent task of depicting our unstable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ recent counterexamples exist . Perhaps the problem of art in the time of climate change is not that its subjects are too immense to be grasped . We might be dealing instead with a lack of artistic imagination , an inability or an unwillingness to adapt the form of the novel to suit the subject . In this respect , Ghost-Eye is more the norm than the exception . But where Ghosh has failed , others might succeed .

@@139144581 <p> At the end of the particularly hot and dry summer of 1910 , a series of lightning storms and human-caused sparks set 1,736 small fires across the northwestern U.S. Hurricane-force winds fanned the flames , merging the fires into a three-million-acre inferno that destroyed several towns and claimed nearly 90 lives . " <p> Known as the " Big Blowup " or the " Big Burn , " the 1910 conflagration is still the largest forest fire in U.S. history , but climate change and the expansion of people into once-wild areas are increasing the risk of damaging blazes . Each year , wildfires in the U.S directly kill about two dozen people on average , cause countless smoke-related illnesses and cost hundreds of billions of dollars . " Your whole life is built around looking out of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Forest Fire Lookout Association and longtime volunteer lookout operator . @@139163181 <h> What India 's young people are saying about families <h> Young Indians still want families , but the conditions they seek reveal their aspirations , anxieties , and changing realities <p> ' The Demographic Futures Survey shows how population data can and must be deployed to help countries understand , plan for and adapt to demographic shifts ' Photo Credit : Getty Images/iStockphoto <p> Ask a grandmother in India what has changed since her time , and she will not talk to you about fertility rates . She will talk about her granddaughter , who finished college , has a city job , and is in no hurry to start a family . She will say it with pride and concern in the same breath , a blend the data reflects too . <h> The UNFPA survey <p> On World Population Day this year ( July 11 ) , UNFPA released the Demographic Futures Survey , the largest study of its kind , with over 1,08,000 young adults surveyed across 73 countries . It asked a simple question : not whether young people still wanted partnership and family , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ year , India 's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare set the theme , " Healthy Timing and Spacing of Pregnancies " or HTSP , a reminder that at the heart of every demographic number is a question of choice : whether young people can decide , freely and on their own timeline , when and how to build their families . ) <p> India 's fertility rate has settled at two children per woman , below the replacement level of 2.1 . Some will hear that and reach for words like " baby bust " or " population crisis " . At UNFPA , we see something else entirely . This is not a warning sign but the outcome of sustained government investment across decades , in girls ' education , the National Health Mission , and expanding contraceptive choice and maternal health services . The share of young women married before 18 years has fallen from 23.3% to 20.1% in just the last few years . That is a policy achievement India 's institutions can rightly take credit for . <p> But numbers tell more than one story @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ news , we miss what young India is trying to say . <h> Related Stories <p> Ask young people directly , and most want what generations before them wanted . Across the country , four in 10 women and a third of men say that two children is their ideal family size . The Demographic Futures Survey found the same pattern across countries : young people are not turning away from family life ; they are asking whether the conditions exist to build it . So why the hesitation here ? When we ask young couples what stands between them and the life they picture , the answers are almost always practical . Money comes first , cited by nearly four in 10 . Then housing . Then job security . Then a very simple , human worry : how well can we care for our children ? <p> That last question falls on one set of shoulders far more than another . Young women in India spend over five hours a day on unpaid housework and caregiving ; young men spend about half an hour . Only 15 in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to 55 in every 100 young men . These are not merely statistics . They help explain why so many capable young women feel that they must choose between a career and a family , when no one should have to choose at all . <h> The climate change issue <p> There is a newer worry layered on top of the old ones . The survey found that nearly all young people say climate change is disrupting their lives , and about half say it affects their peace of mind . Nearly half of young Indians also report being very worried about conflict , economic insecurity and environmental risk all at once , among the higher rates recorded anywhere . Add high youth unemployment and a mental health conversation that is only beginning in many Indian households , and a fuller picture emerges . This is not a generation rejecting parenthood . It is a generation asking , quite reasonably , whether the ground beneath it is steady enough to build on . <p> India is also marked by inter-State disparity . Bihar 's fertility rate stands at 2.7 , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and Tamil Nadu have long settled below the replacement level , while Bihar , Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand are still catching up . These differences show that India 's demographic transition is unfolding at different speeds across States , and that no single national policy can fully address every State 's realities . <h> Responding to youth aspiration <p> The UNFPA 's partnership with the Indian government and communities is aimed at translating what young people are telling us into practical support : high-quality , affordable and accessible childcare ; families that share caregiving more equally ; continued investment in stable , dignified work for young people entering the labour force ; and greater attention to youth mental health , including climate anxiety , in conversations about family and the future . The private sector also has a vital role to play through parental leave , flexible work arrangements and family-friendly workplaces that enable young people to balance work and caregiving . The UNFPA has a unique role in the United Nations development system as a leader in data collection , population dynamics and evidence-based policymaking . The Demographic Futures @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to help countries understand , plan for and adapt to demographic shifts . <p> India is home to 255 million young people aged 15 to 24 years , the largest generation this country , or perhaps any country , has ever raised . This is India 's demographic dividend , a window of opportunity that will not remain open indefinitely . The choices we make today will determine whether this generation can fully realise its potential before that window begins to close . Young Indians are not walking away from the idea of family . They are waiting for the conditions that would let them say yes to it fully . <p> Andrea M. @@139193587 <h> The Hindu 's weekly Science for All newsletter explains all things Science , without the jargon . <p> As spring approaches in the hyper-biodiverse Himalayas , birds that are accustomed to cooler climes migrate to the north . This is driven not just by temperature or precipitation alone , but also the availability of prey : arthropods ( insects and spiders ) . But climate change is altering the rhythm of this dynamic . <p> Scientists at the Centre for Ecological Sciences , Indian Institute of Science ( IISc ) , Bengaluru , set out to study the phenomenon in Arunachal Pradesh 's Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary and understand the changing patterns in insect availability and avian migration through seasons . <p> Arthropods at higher elevations might emerge earlier in the year in response to the advanced onset of summer as a result of climate change , Umesh Srinivasan , associate professor , Centre for Ecological Sciences , IISc , told The Hindu . " However , many species of birds might not use temperature as a cue to migrate upwards , but might use cues such as day-length , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ he added , " migratory birds might move to reach higher elevations on a ' normal schedule ' , only to find that the peak in arthropod abundance has already abated , leaving them with suboptimal resource availability . " <p> Climate change brings about spring early , and the abundance of arthropods also peaks earlier , Tarun Menon , lead author told Nature India . " This can have detrimental effects for migratory birds , especially the insect-eating and ground-feeding birds , " he added . <p> They found that arthropods , which most of the world 's birds rely on are " highly sensitive to temperature " , but also , in the mountains , where most terrestrial birds live , the variation in their abundance is likely to influence bird movement . The study was reported in the paper Biology Letters , A Royal Society journal . <p> For the study , scientists sampled arthropods and birds , in summer and winter , across a 2,300 mt forested elevation gradient . They found that in summer , both aerial and terrestrial arthropod numbers increased with elevation in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Arthropods are highly sensitive to climate , and in mountain ranges such as the Himalayas , winter frost " may force most arthropods into a state of dormancy called diapause , " the paper says . " This is likely to cause their relative abundance to decline at high elevations in winter " <p> The scientists sampled 12,744 arthropods in summer and 4,079 in winter , using sticky traps . Their abundance increased with elevation in summer but reduced during the winter . As many as 1,971 birds belonging to 160 species were captured with fine nets in summer and 1,721 , belonging to 133 species in winter . <p> This is the first time that seasonal and elevational changes in arthropod richness has been related to the movement of montane birds . <h> Comments <p> Comments have to be in English , and in full sentences . The strain is testing the adaptations that municipalities have put in place since a hallmark deadly heat wave in 2003 . <p> Repeated bouts of extreme heat led Western Europe to its warmest June on record , according to the European Union 's Copernicus Climate Change Service . The second half of the month had a heat wave that was so intense that it broke monthly and all-time temperature records across several countries . An analysis by the World Weather Attribution ( WWA ) research group found that these extreme temperatures would 've @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ warming and that such temperatures were now about 10 times more likely than they would 've been in 2003 . Heat waves themselves are also hotter than they were in the past : conditions like those of Europe 's June heat wave have become up to 2.5 degrees Celsius warmer than they were decades ago , and the event exposed 327 million people and $15.6 trillion in assets to climate-intensified heat , according to an analysis by the research organization ClimaMeter . <p> That heat has taken a heavy human toll . The European mortality monitoring network backed by the World Health Organization and the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control recorded more than 16,000 excess deaths across 27 European countries during the week of June 22 -- 28 alone , with more than 14,000 of those deaths among people age 65 and older . By purchasing a subscription @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today . <p> Those tallies are almost certainly undercounts : in 2022 the World Health Organization 's real-time estimate put Europe 's heat-related death toll at roughly 15,000 , while a later study in Nature Medicine that worked from full mortality records put the true figure above 61,000 -- more than four times higher than the initial count . The reason for the discrepancy is that heat deaths are typically logged only when a death certificate names heatstroke directly , an approach that misses the much larger toll of heart attacks , strokes and respiratory failures that extreme temperatures trigger in people with existing conditions . Public health researchers have warned that undercounting delays the enactment of better protections because it leads officials and the public to underestimate how lethal heat is until the retrospective data catch up months or years later . <p> And heat 's damage is n't limited to the time during a heat wave . These losses , layered onto existing global supply strain , could push up food prices . @@139282395 <p> Sitting at the Environmental Protection Agency with a mix of CEOs and cabinet officials , President Trump announced this week that a group of more than 200 stakeholders including governors , utility companies , and data center developers had signed up for his Ratepayer Protection Pledge , vowing to protect consumers from the rising costs of electricity . <p> The announcement is an attempt to hold off the growing anxiety over electricity bills , which are on the rise in part because of the AI-driven infrastructure buildout . And the slower policymakers are to take decisive , substantive action , the more likely it becomes that today 's targeted fixes give way to demands for wholesale restructuring . <p> Two days before Trump launched his updated pledge , I moderated a panel at the Aspen Ideas Climate summit in Chicago addressing issues of rising electricity costs and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ came over the needed scale of solutions . <p> Allison Clements , a former member of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission , argued that states and utilities should move quickly to insulate customers from the cost of data centers , citing a range of regulatory tweaks . @@139284081 <h> Wind Or Solar : Which Energy Source Is More Efficient ? <p> Wind energy and solar energy are the twin standard bearers of the renewable energy movement . They are both in abundant supply and produce no greenhouse gases once installed , leading to better air quality and paving the way to curbing global warming . They are also more affordable now in most places than fossil fuels , which are subject to highly volatile price shifts . Wind and solar are superior to oil and coal in almost every single way , but how do they stack up to each other ? While both are productive in their own right , wind holds the edge for a very simple reason . <p> Turbines convert roughly half of the wind energy passing through them into electricity , but solar panels only convert around a fifth of the solar energy that hits them into electricity . As it stands , wind turbine technology is simply more efficient than solar array technology . However , it could be argued that energy efficiency is only one part of the overall efficiency of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hard to compare because they are each suited to totally different needs . <h> Pros and cons of wind power <p> Pituk Loonhong/Getty Images <p> Aside from the efficiency of turbines over solar arrays , the next biggest advantage that wind energy has is availability . Modern turbines can generate electricity from wind speeds as low as 6 mph , which is classified by the National Weather Service as a " light breeze " . Electricity production scales up with wind speed and only cuts off if winds become dangerously strong . Changes in wind speed are typically gradual and predictable , unlike shut downs at power plants . <p> Wind turbine technology has been steadily advancing to harness even greater amounts of power . In the past two decades , wind turbines have grown 59% taller on average , according to the World Economic Forum . This number is significant because wind speeds are stronger higher above ground . Objects on the ground , like buildings and trees , impede the flow of wind , slowing it down and offering less power for turbines to harness . For that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ big ones going up in China ) are going to be a key part of the energy sector going forward . <p> The big drawback to wind energy is that you ca n't put a wind turbine just anywhere . They need to be clear of obstacles and they generate too much noise to be close to communities . Although they are more efficient than solar panels , they are n't as versatile or easy to install . For these reasons , wind power is almost exclusively used on the industrial scale , and not for home installation ( although some small home turbines do exist ) . <h> Pros and cons of solar power <p> Jamil Yasin/Shutterstock <p> Solar energy is not only less efficient than wind energy , but it 's also less available . While it only takes a light breeze for a wind turbine to start producing electricity , solar arrays can only gather power when they receive direct sunlight . This means they have to be oriented very particularly to face the sun , and they wo n't work at night or in heavily overcast @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ efficiency , might have you thinking that solar is a total waste , but it has some sneaky advantages over wind power as well . <p> On the other hand , another downside to solar energy is the fact that solar panels are made with silicon and various rare metals that are obtained by mining . The mining industry is a major contributor to climate change , so manufacturing solar panels does come at a notable cost . With this in mind , on top of all else we 've covered here , it 's clear that wind is the king of clean energy .

Canada 's forests , the argument goes , are simply too vast and too remote to manage . Its dense stands of black spruce and jack pine evolved to burn in intense fires that destroy the main canopy and reset ecosystems . Once flames reach the treetops , a " crown fire " can race across the canopy too hot and fast for firefighters to attack directly . <p> There 's some truth to that . Fire seasons have lasted longer in recent years . But neither Canada nor the United States is condemned to a future of smoke-choked skies . Policy choices shape how large and destructive fires become . Both @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reduce fire risk . Now Canadians and Americans alike are paying the price . <p> And it 's a steep price . Wildfire smoke carries fine particulate matter small enough to lodge deep in the lungs and enter the bloodstream . It aggravates asthma and raises the risk of heart attacks and strokes . A 2025 Nature study estimated that smoke from Canada 's record 2023 fires contributed to thousands of deaths in the United States . <p> Fortunately , Canada and the United States have tools to reduce the danger . The media and politicians are quick to blame climate change , but the reality is that forest management works . Fuel treatments such as thinning , brush clearance and prescribed burning remove small trees , brush and dead material that allow flames to climb into the canopy and explode into a dangerous crown fire . <p> The evidence in western US forests is hard to dismiss . A 2024 Forest Service meta-analysis found that thinning followed by prescribed fire reduced the severity of later wildfires by 72% on average . Crews stopped the fire after it advanced about 400 feet into the treatment . In an Alaska experiment , another crown fire became a surface fire within about 100 feet of entering a treated zone . <p> Such treatments can save entire communities . The Westbank First Nation in British Columbia has long used thinning and controlled burning . Fanned by strong winds , the blaze ripped through the Rocky Mountain National Park , closing major roads , destroying hundreds of homes and blanketing the area in a thick cloud of smoke . <p> Dubbed The East Troublesome @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ making it one of the state 's largest blazes in history -- and killed two people . <p> After the fire , aerial photos showed vast swathes of the forest burnt to ash . But surrounding the devastation remained a green oasis that managed to escape the blaze , all thanks to the humble beaver . <p> Beavers build dams , dig channels and transform small streams into broad wetland areas . This helps keep plants lush and green , even throughout long periods of drought . <p> It means when a wildfire ignites , the green vegetation near the beaver ponds will be much harder to burn compared to dried-out areas . <p> Experts say that fires will often take the path of least resistance , burning through dry vegetation away from beaver ponds instead of trying to smolder through the wet areas . <p> This creates a safe refuge for animals that may be unable to escape a wildfire , such as frogs , small mammals , and fish . <p> Infographic showing how green corridors can stay green during wildfires due to beaver activity.Emily Fairfax <p> A @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vegetation data from five large wildfires across the western US to explore how effectively beavers can build climate-resilient landscapes . <p> It found that beaver-dammed corridors are " relatively unaffected " by wildfire when compared to regions without beaver presence . On average , plant health in areas without beavers declined about three times more during wildfires than in areas with beavers . <p> A later study published in the National Library of Medicine last year modelled the potential impacts beavers could have in California 's Sierra Nevada , a region at high risk of drought and wildfire . <p> Researchers found that 51 per cent of beaver dam-building capacity remains in this region compared to historical levels , and " considerable " dam capacity remains in all watersheds . This is an area of land that channels rain and snowmelt to a common water body , effectively acting like a giant funnel . <p> The study " conservatively " estimates that beaver dams have the potential to store a total of 120 million cubic metres of surface water and create 2,200 square kilometres of fire resilience in high fire @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have the potential to create the greatest water and fire benefits due to physical landscape and habitat characteristics are frequently found within watersheds that are at high risk for both drought and fire , " the study says . <p> " Even in areas where fire and drought are less probable , the reestablishment of beavers will likely provide similar benefits . Maybe never in my lifetime , but they are definitely going to be more warm-water exotics that will make their way on the Cape as the years go on , " Rouette said . <p> ( Copyright ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This material may not be published , broadcast , rewritten , or redistributed. )
